question: Can an LLM that is empirically unable to solve a hard math subset nevertheless generate question-answer training data that moves a copy of itself off the sparse-reward RLVR plateau, and is rewarding the generator by measured student progress more stable and useful than intrinsic learnability rewards?

key_findings.claim: Author method: SOAR instantiates curriculum generation as black-box bilevel optimization rather than differentiating through student training.
key_findings.evidence: A teacher and student begin from the same base model. The teacher samples sets of synthetic question-answer pairs; separate student copies receive ten RLOO updates on each set; greedy accuracy improvement on sampled hard training questions becomes the set-level reward for an outer RLOO teacher update. Because the outer update treats downstream improvement as a scalar reward, it avoids backpropagating through the inner optimizer.

key_findings.claim: Author mechanism: teacher rewards are explicitly grounded in a fixed target failure set, but they are noisy selected estimates rather than progress guarantees.
key_findings.evidence: For each candidate dataset X_k, the reward is the trained student's greedy accuracy on 64 sampled D_train questions minus the baseline student's accuracy, averaged over four independent inner trainings. Promotion chooses the highest-reward dataset and the median-reward student within it once a three-step moving-average reward exceeds 0.01. This reduces variance but still selects a winner from four datasets on a resampled, finite reward panel.

key_findings.claim: Author proposition: format-based rejection sampling leaves the grouped RLOO gradient expressible using proposal-policy log gradients.
key_findings.evidence: For a parameter-independent acceptance set S, log pi(z)=log pi_0(z)-log pi_0(S). The normalization-gradient term cancels because leave-one-out advantages sum to zero. The result is specific to RLOO and the paper expressly says it does not hold for plain REINFORCE; it also does not validate the mathematical content of accepted questions.

anchors.section: B.2 Parsing Teacher Outputs and Proposition 1

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: fail@128 is a finite screening label, not evidence that each retained problem has zero solution probability or lies outside the base model's capability support.
key_findings.evidence: Problems are retained after one batch of 128 failures at temperature 1.0. On the held-out MATH subset the same base model later obtains 0.3% pass@1 and 7.5% pass@32, and analogous nonzero results occur on HARP and OlympiadBench; the authors attribute this to different stochastic seeds. The experiments therefore establish a low-success empirical plateau under a particular screen, not literal impossibility.

key_findings.claim: Author result: on MATH fail@128, promotion questions and the promoted student substantially outperform direct hard-only training at every reported inference budget.
key_findings.evidence: At pass@1/4/8/16/32, Hard-Only reports 0.5/1.7/3.2/5.7/9.6%, SOAR-PQ 1.7/5.3/8.5/13.0/18.9%, and SOAR-PS 1.0/3.8/6.8/11.5/18.1%. PQ is also above SeRL at both reported checkpoints and Intrinsic-T, while remaining below the full-MATH curated upper bound at pass@32 (22.0%). Standard deviations are large for several methods, including PQ pass@32 18.9 +/- 5.3 and the four-times-larger Hard-Only group 12.4 +/- 7.4.

key_findings.claim: Author result: HARP gains are smaller but consistent in the reported means, and generated questions can outperform an equal-sized curated HARP sample.
key_findings.evidence: Hard-Only versus SOAR-PQ is 0.4 versus 0.7% pass@1 and 8.2 versus 12.3% pass@32; PS reaches 11.8% pass@32 and SeRL step 100 reaches 10.9%. A random 128-question HARP training subset reaches only 8.7% pass@32, whereas a random 128-question MATH subset reaches 11.9% and the full MATH train set reaches 16.2%.

anchors.section: Table 5 HARP pass@k and oracle-data comparison

key_findings.claim: Author result: MATH- and HARP-trained curricula transfer to the held-out OlympiadBench split, with HARP-derived PQ strongest among the proposed variants.
key_findings.evidence: At pass@32, Hard-Only is 6.9 +/- 2.7%, PQ-MATH 10.6 +/- 2.7%, PQ-HARP 12.0 +/- 3.0%, PS-HARP 11.7 +/- 1.6%, and a random 128-question MATH subset 14.6 +/- 1.4%. The OOD claim is therefore supported relative to Hard-Only and HARP-128, but the strongest curated MATH comparison remains better.

key_findings.claim: Author result: the trained teacher's improved pedagogical distribution does not improve its own direct problem solving.
key_findings.evidence: Direct inference with Grounded-T is statistically close to base inference: on MATH pass@32 it is 8.3 +/- 1.1% versus 7.5 +/- 1.3%, and on HARP 6.8 +/- 0.7% versus 6.4%. The useful effect instead appears when another student is trained on generated questions, supporting a teaching/solving dissociation in this setup.

anchors.section: Table 5 and inference with trained teacher

key_findings.claim: Author result with limited seed support: target-grounded teachers are more stable and more semantically diverse than learnability-reward teachers.
key_findings.evidence: Across four Grounded-T teachers per dataset and three Intrinsic-T teachers, one intrinsic seed produces student collapse across datasets while grounded seeds give similar trajectories. Vendi Score on 128-question standardized samples is 34.91 for Base-T, 34.66 for Grounded-T-HARP, 31.99 for Grounded-T-MATH, 28.33 for PQ, and 10.82 for Intrinsic-T. These are small teacher-level samples despite many downstream student runs.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the evidence does not isolate the causal claim that incorrect answers help, or that structure matters more than correctness.
key_findings.evidence: The controlled comparison trains on 82 correct-only PQ-HARP items versus 144 well-posed items, where the latter strictly contains the former plus 62 additional examples. Better performance can therefore arise from more questions, broader topic coverage, or more updates rather than incorrect labels themselves. The oracle labels also come from one Claude-4.5-Sonnet judgment pipeline without human validation. The experiment supports that a mixed set containing incorrect answers can help, not that incorrectness is beneficial or correctness is less important ceteris paribus.

anchors.section: C.5 Do Incorrect Synthetic Questions Help?

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: 'without additional curated data' still requires a curated, answer-keyed target set and an automatic verifier for student rewards.
key_findings.evidence: The teacher never receives the hard question text in its prompt, and generated answers need not be correct, but the outer reward evaluates greedy student answers on D_train against ground-truth answers using Math-Verify. SOAR removes curated intermediate curricula and synthetic-question verification; it does not remove target questions, target labels, or verifiable target-domain evaluation.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the extra-compute baselines do not match SOAR's end-to-end compute, so they do not rule out compute as a general explanation.
key_findings.evidence: Each SOAR teacher run uses 32 H100/H200 GPUs for roughly 48-60 hours, plus repeated inner students; each fresh-student evaluation uses eight GPUs for about 12 hours. The direct controls are only a four-times RLOO group-size run on MATH and a 6500-step Hard-Only extension on HARP. They show that those two reallocations fail, but are not FLOP-, sample-, wall-time-, or hyperparameter-matched to the nested meta-RL system.

key_findings.claim: Author negative result: a synthetic-first curriculum is unstable on HARP and OlympiadBench, so the evaluation protocol switches to mixed real/synthetic training.
key_findings.evidence: On those two datasets, curriculum training exhibits an early spike followed by a sharp performance crash and lower convergence than mixing; only MATH uses the synthetic warm-start because Base-T performed better under that choice. Thus a core curriculum-shaped deployment is not robust across the tested targets, and the reported protocol is dataset-dependent.

key_findings.claim: Author negative result: separating question and answer generation into two turns performs worse and yields at most one promotion.
key_findings.evidence: Across four teacher seeds and both n=32 and n=64, the multi-turn reward quickly plateaus; every reported pass@k row is below the default single-turn results. This shows the method is sensitive to generation/credit-assignment format rather than being an invariant consequence of the progress reward.

anchors.section: D.3 Problem Generation Format and Table 8

key_findings.claim: Author scaling check exposes a boundary: the 8B model improves, but the promotion mechanism never activates under transferred 3B hyperparameters.
key_findings.evidence: For Llama-3.1-8B, Grounded-T reaches 13.7 +/- 2.7% MATH pass@32 versus 9.1 +/- 3.2% Hard-Only, yet neither of two teacher seeds produces a promotion. The result supports usefulness of a trained teacher distribution at 8B, not scaling of the full adaptive promotion loop.

anchors.section: D.4 Model Size, Table 9 and Figure 18

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the headline stability and plateau-escape conclusions are empirical and conditional, not formal guarantees of sustained self-improvement.
key_findings.evidence: The sole theorem concerns RLOO rejection sampling. Teacher checkpoints, early stopping, mixing strategy, reward threshold, dataset size, and finite horizon are selected empirically; grounded teachers are tested on only two math source datasets, mostly one 3B model, and at most four promotions. No theorem bounds generalization, reward overfitting, monotonic student progress, or long-run collapse.

method.core_idea: Train a question-generating teacher by rewarding synthetic datasets according to the measured improvement they induce in a separately trained student on a fixed, answer-keyed hard target set.
method.mechanism: At each outer iteration the teacher samples four 64-item candidate datasets after format rejection. Four student replicas per dataset receive short RLOO training, and their average greedy-accuracy gain on 64 sampled target-training questions is assigned to all items in that dataset for an outer RLOO update. When a moving-average reward threshold is crossed, the median student trained on the best dataset becomes the new baseline and that dataset is accumulated as Promotion Questions. Final evaluation either runs the promoted student or trains fresh students on promotion/teacher-sampled questions plus real hard questions.
assumptions: A finite 0/128 sampling screen identifies a useful sparse-reward plateau even though later base-model samples can succeed.
The answer-keyed hard training split is representative of the held-out hard split and is permissible as a black-box grounding signal.
Greedy accuracy gain on 64 sampled reward questions after 10-20 inner steps is a sufficiently stable estimate of dataset utility.
Averaging four student replicas and selecting the median student controls inner-loop noise enough for outer RLOO.
The format acceptance set used for rejection sampling is parameter-independent, as required by Proposition 1.
Questions whose proposed answers are wrong can still yield useful RL updates through structural or distributional cues.
Math-Verify and the tiered 120/20/10/0 student reward reliably score target and synthetic answers.
Teacher checkpoint times, promotion threshold, candidate-set size, and dataset-specific mixing choices transfer beyond the initial tuning runs.
MATH, HARP, and OlympiadBench hard subsets capture the relevant sparse-binary-reward regime.
Nested teacher/student seed aggregation is adequate despite only two to four independent teacher seeds per key comparison.
The enormous nested-training compute is an acceptable proof-of-concept cost and does not itself explain gains through an untested allocation.
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and the limited 8B ablation are informative about broader model scaling.

techniques.role: Uses downstream accuracy change on a fixed target failure set as the teacher's curriculum reward.
Runs short student RLOO inside an outer teacher RLOO loop without differentiating through training.
Averages four student-training rewards for each candidate dataset to reduce variance.
Advances the baseline student and accumulates the best dataset after a moving-average reward threshold.
Filters teacher generations for tags, boxed answers, and parseability while retaining the grouped RLOO gradient identity.
Constructs low-initial-success train/test subsets from MATH, HARP, and OlympiadBench.
Separates data utility from a lucky promotion trajectory by training fresh base students on accumulated questions.
Aggregates variation across independent teacher runs and multiple downstream student runs.
Measures generated-question diversity, oracle-judged well-posedness/correctness, and per-teacher stability.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on a 360-problem held-out MATH fail@128 split
evaluations.metric: Pass@1, 4, 8, 16, and 32, aggregated over nested seeds
evaluations.result: SOAR-PQ reaches 1.7/5.3/8.5/13.0/18.9% versus Hard-Only 0.5/1.7/3.2/5.7/9.6%; PS reaches 18.1% pass@32 and full curated MATH reaches 22.0%.
evaluations.baseline: Base inference, Hard-Only at group sizes 32 and 128, SeRL, Intrinsic-T, direct Grounded-T inference, sampled curated HARP/MATH, and full MATH.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on a 714-problem held-out HARP fail@128 split
evaluations.result: SOAR-PQ reaches 12.3 +/- 2.0% pass@32 versus Hard-Only 8.2 +/- 1.0%, SeRL-100 10.9 +/- 0.4%, and Intrinsic-T 9.6 +/- 2.1%.
evaluations.baseline: The same families as MATH, plus 128-item and full curated-data comparisons.

evaluations.setting: Held-out 158-problem OlympiadBench fail@128 split not used for teacher training
evaluations.result: PQ-HARP reaches 12.0 +/- 3.0% pass@32 and PQ-MATH 10.6 +/- 2.7% versus Hard-Only 6.9 +/- 2.7%; random MATH-128 reaches 14.6 +/- 1.4%.
evaluations.baseline: Hard-Only, PQ/PS/Grounded-T from both teacher domains, Intrinsic-T, and curated HARP/MATH samples.

evaluations.setting: Question distributions from Base-T, Grounded-T, PQ, and Intrinsic-T
evaluations.metric: Qwen3-8B-embedding Vendi Score after bootstrap standardization to 128 questions
evaluations.result: Grounded-T-HARP/MATH scores 34.66/31.99 versus Base-T 34.91, PQ 28.33, and Intrinsic-T 10.82.
evaluations.baseline: Base and intrinsic teacher distributions; uncertainty is bootstrap-over-question rather than many independent teachers.

evaluations.setting: Claude-4.5-Sonnet taxonomy over 375-384 generated questions per source and HARP subset retraining
evaluations.metric: Well-posedness, proposed-answer correctness, error type, and pass@k
evaluations.result: PQ is 64.6% well-posed and 32.8% correct; Grounded-T is 70.0%/36.5%, Intrinsic-T 63.5%/55.5%. A 144-item well-posed set beats its 82-item correct-only subset, but item count and coverage are confounded.
evaluations.baseline: Base-T, Intrinsic-T, Grounded-T, and correct-only versus superset well-posed training.

evaluations.metric: Pass@k after four-times-larger MATH RLOO groups or 6500 HARP Hard-Only steps
evaluations.result: Larger MATH groups reach 12.4 +/- 7.4% pass@32 and extended HARP training does not improve; neither control is matched to total SOAR compute.

evaluations.setting: Teacher-objective and promotion ablations across downstream fresh students
evaluations.result: Grounded-T generally leads to more consistent trajectories; one of three Intrinsic-T teachers collapses across datasets, and Grounded-T without promotion underperforms full Grounded-T.
evaluations.baseline: Base-T, Intrinsic-T, and Grounded-T without promotion.

evaluations.result: Two-turn question/answer generation reaches at most one promotion and is worse in every Table 8 row; synthetic-first training crashes on HARP/OlympiadBench, while mixed training is stable.
evaluations.baseline: Default single-turn generation and dataset-specific mixed/curriculum schedules.

evaluations.setting: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MATH fail@128 with untuned 3B hyperparameters
evaluations.metric: Pass@k over two teacher by two student seeds
evaluations.result: Grounded-T reaches 13.7 +/- 2.7% pass@32 versus Hard-Only 9.1 +/- 3.2%, but no student promotions occur.

limitations: The target curriculum reward requires curated hard questions, ground-truth answers, and automatic answer verification; the method is only intermediate-data-free.
A 0/128 screen is a noisy finite-sample selection event, and later base inference has nonzero success on every retained benchmark.
Main evidence is confined to mathematical RLVR, one 3B model, a lightly tested 8B model, and two teacher-training domains.
Only four main teacher seeds per domain and three teacher seeds for key objective ablations support broad stability claims.
The incorrect-answer experiment changes dataset size from 82 to 144 and therefore cannot identify answer incorrectness as the beneficial factor.
Teacher reward uses a small resampled target panel and selects the best of multiple candidate datasets, creating winner-selection noise and potential target-train overfitting.
Teacher/student checkpoint selection, early stopping, curriculum-versus-mix choice, and evaluation windows are empirically chosen and dataset-dependent.
SOAR is extremely expensive: each teacher run uses 32 H100/H200 GPUs for about 48-60 hours before downstream evaluation.
Compute controls test only two alternative allocations and are not matched to the full nested procedure.
The 8B run produces no promotion, leaving the central adaptive mechanism unvalidated at that scale.
The paper does not evaluate code, natural language, open-ended tasks, noisy target labels, or targets without verifiers.
No formal result guarantees monotonic progress, generalization to D_test, robustness to reward sampling, or avoidance of long-horizon collapse.
failure_modes: Intrinsic learnability reward can collapse teacher diversity and produce a teacher whose questions cause downstream student collapse.
A synthetic-first curriculum can spike and then abruptly crash on HARP and OlympiadBench; mixing is required there.
Multi-turn question/answer generation plateaus early and largely prevents student promotions.
Promotion can fail entirely when hyperparameters are transferred to an 8B model.
Incorrect or ambiguous synthetic answers can directly reinforce wrong outputs under the teacher-provided answer key.
Small reward panels and best-of-group selection can promote a dataset that benefited from inner-loop or evaluation noise.
The teacher can specialize to the fixed target training split without acquiring general solving ability; direct teacher inference shows essentially no gain.
Hard-Only performance can deteriorate late in training, making fixed-budget comparisons and checkpoint selection consequential.
Sampling only 32 or 64 questions from Grounded-T yields higher downstream variance than sampling 128.
Format rejection can become expensive or biased if the teacher policy produces few parseable boxed answers, even though Proposition 1 handles the conditional gradient.
reusable_insights: Reward a data generator with measured downstream learner improvement when proxy notions of difficulty are vulnerable to gaming.
Separate data quality from a fortunate learner trajectory by retraining fresh learners on accumulated generated data.
Use replicated inner trainings and median promotion to reduce bilevel reward noise, while separately auditing best-of-group selection bias.
Treat finite failure screens as low-success strata rather than proof of zero capability, and always report later base-model pass@k.
Audit curriculum schedule itself: generated data may work as a mixture even when an intuitive easy-to-hard warm-start crashes.
Measure generator diversity across independent policies, not only pooled outputs, because one proxy-reward seed can collapse catastrophically.
When testing noisy labels, equalize example count and question distribution so label correctness is not confounded with added coverage.
Distinguish removal of curated intermediate data from removal of target supervision; a target-progress reward still consumes labels and a verifier.
Report teacher-level replication and total end-to-end compute separately from the much larger count of nested student runs.
open_questions: Does the progress-grounded reward remain stable over many more promotions, or eventually overfit/collapse like intrinsic self-play?
Can a cheaper influence estimate or learned reward proxy preserve target grounding without training dozens of inner students per outer step?
Would a target-train/target-validation split inside the outer loop prevent winner's-curse promotions and improve held-out generalization?
Do size-matched well-posed questions with deliberately wrong answers help more than equally diverse questions with corrected answers?
Which features of generated questions—topic coverage, difficulty, syntax, reasoning pattern, or answer distribution—actually mediate the gain?
Can promotions be made to work reliably at 8B and larger scales without model-specific sweeps?
How does SOAR compare under a strictly matched compute envelope with more direct RLVR samples, rejection sampling, active data selection, or curated synthesis?
Can target-grounded curricula be learned when only preference, partial-credit, or non-verifiable target feedback is available?
How sensitive are results to target-set contamination in pretraining and to the particular fail@128 screen seed?
Do generated curricula transfer beyond math to code, formal proof, science, or open-ended language tasks?
Can the teacher condition explicitly on student state without exposing target questions and thereby avoid repeatedly rediscovering obsolete curricula?

competitive_landscape.title: CPMobius: Iterative Coach-Player Reasoning for Data-Free Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: The closest current primary competitor: a coach proposes reasoning tasks and is rewarded from changes in a player's performance in an iterative cooperative RL loop.
competitive_landscape.difference: CPMobius directly overlaps the broad coach/teacher-by-student-improvement idea and is an accepted ICML 2026 paper. It claims no external training data during co-evolution and uses difficulty/player-success shaping, whereas SOAR deliberately uses progress on a fixed answer-keyed fail@128 target set as the grounding signal, short replicated inner trainings, and thresholded student promotion.

competitive_landscape.title: Absolute Zero: Reinforced Self-play Reasoning with Zero Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct zero-data self-play reasoning system in which a model proposes and solves its own tasks with RLVR.
competitive_landscape.difference: Absolute Zero uses a code executor to validate proposed tasks and verify answers and rewards task learnability without a fixed target-failure reward. SOAR targets math domains lacking synthetic-question verification and accepts noisy proposed answers, but consumes labeled hard target questions to measure actual student progress.

competitive_landscape.title: R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: A challenger-solver co-evolution framework that autonomously generates a near-frontier curriculum without pre-existing tasks or labels.
competitive_landscape.difference: R-Zero trains distinct challenger and solver roles around intrinsic edge-of-capability rewards and evaluates multiple general/math backbones. SOAR instead anchors generator utility to post-update accuracy on a pre-existing hard target set and emphasizes escape from a screened sparse-reward plateau.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Questioning Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: An asymmetric proposer-solver self-play system that generates its own questions and answers for reasoning improvement.
competitive_landscape.difference: SQLM rewards proposer questions for intermediate difficulty and uses majority vote as the solver's correctness proxy, with unit tests in code. SOAR directly ablates this learnability style and replaces it with measured progress on labeled hard target problems, at far greater bilevel compute cost.

competitive_landscape.title: SeRL: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models with Limited Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: A self-instruction/self-rewarding RL system that evolves a reasoning curriculum from a limited seed set and filters for quality, diversity, and difficulty.
competitive_landscape.difference: SeRL uses majority-vote pseudo-rewards and online filters and was run by SOAR as a direct MATH/HARP baseline. SOAR uses the seed set only as a hidden downstream progress evaluator and reports higher pass@k on its selected Llama-3.2-3B fail@128 setup.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Self-Play For Data-Free Training
competitive_landscape.relationship: A game-theoretic language self-play method for improving instruction following, math, and coding without additional data.
competitive_landscape.difference: Language Self-Play casts capabilities as competitive language-game performance and does not optimize generated curricula against a fixed target failure set. SOAR is a specialized teacher-student data-generation loop whose outer signal is supervised target-domain improvement.

competitive_landscape.title: SAGE: Multi-Agent Self-Evolution for LLM Reasoning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later multi-agent self-evolution system with challenger, planner, solver, and critic roles, explicit curriculum generation, and verifier-based quality control.
competitive_landscape.difference: SAGE adds planning and criticism to prevent curriculum drift and uses a small seed plus external verifiers across math and code. SOAR has only teacher/student roles and allows wrong synthetic answers, but its target-progress reward directly tests whether a short student update helps the fixed hard distribution.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Adapting Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: A bilevel self-adaptation method that trains a model to generate finetuning data/update directives using downstream performance after adaptation as the RL reward.
competitive_landscape.difference: SEAL is the closest conceptual precedent for rewarding self-generated updates by post-update task performance, but it conditions self-edits on provided knowledge or examples and studies SFT-based adaptation. SOAR generates standalone math curricula without seeing target questions and uses nested RLVR plus a promoted student baseline.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first LLM self-play curriculum grounded in a concrete target failure regime rather than an intrinsic difficulty proxy, the first 'double meta-RL loop' of this kind for LLM self-play, and evidence that a model can generate useful stepping stones for problems it cannot solve.
novelty_assessment.evidence: SOAR combines outer RLOO on generated datasets, replicated inner student RLOO, a fixed hard-set progress reward, and thresholded student promotion; on screened MATH/HARP plateaus it beats Hard-Only, intrinsic-teacher, and SeRL comparisons and transfers to OlympiadBench.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest defensible novelty is the specific target-grounded implementation and its fail@128 empirical study, not the broad teacher/coach rewarded by learner improvement. Self-Adapting Language Models already uses downstream post-adaptation performance as an RL signal, and current ICML 2026 CPMobius independently presents a very close coach-player progress-reward loop. Absolute Zero, R-Zero, SQLM, SeRL, and Language Self-Play already cover autonomous proposer-solver curricula. SOAR remains distinctive in hiding the fixed answer-keyed target questions from the teacher while using short measured target progress—not synthetic correctness or intermediate difficulty—to select noisy question-answer sets and advance a baseline student. The causal claim that wrong answers help and the general claim of stable frontier expansion should be narrowed to the tested, compute-heavy math setting.
